  hungry."
  
  When the woman had gone, a little after eleven, with a warm bag under her arm, Ines went back to the proofing cabinet and lifted the cloth from the jar on the top
  shelf. The starter had risen during the night, bubbling gently, the surface domed and full of tiny pockets of air. It smelled sharp and sweet and faintly sour,
  like fruit and yeast and something older than both.
  
  She fed it a spoonful of flour and a spoonful of water, stirred it slowly, and set it back in its place.
  
  That evening, when the shutters were down and the ovens were cooling, Ines sat on an upturned crate in the back room with a cup of tea and wrote in the notebook
  she kept beside the flour bins. It was not a recipe book. It was a list of names: the customers who came every week, the ones who had moved away, the twins, the
  woman in the green coat, a boy from the Thursday class who had shaped his first perfect boule and looked as if he had been handed a medal.
  
  Below the names, she wrote the date, and then, after a moment's thought, a single line.
  
  The bread is still here. So are we.
  
  She closed the notebook, switched off the last light, and walked home through the empty streets with the smell of the day still clinging to her coat. Behind her,
  in the dark bakery, the jar on the top shelf went on quietly doing what it had always done, turning flour and water into something that could feed people, one day
  at a time.
